passage.title: Modern Music Consumption Trends
passage.text:
The way people listen to music has changed more dramatically in the past twenty years than in almost any other period in the history of recorded sound. From the early days of vinyl records and cassette tapes to the rise of compact discs in the 1980s and 1990s, each new format brought changes to how music was bought and enjoyed. But none of these earlier shifts compare to the transformation that digital technology and the internet have brought about in the twenty-first century. Today, billions of people around the world listen to music through streaming services on their smartphones, tablets, and computers, and the idea of physically owning a music collection has become unfamiliar to an entire generation of young listeners.

Streaming platforms such as Spotify, Apple Music, and YouTube Music have become the dominant way that most people access music in countries where reliable internet connections are widely available. These services allow users to listen to tens of millions of songs on demand for a monthly subscription fee, or for free with occasional advertisements. The convenience of having an almost unlimited library of music available at any moment, from any location, has made streaming enormously popular with people of all ages. According to industry reports, global music streaming revenues have grown every year for the past decade, and streaming now accounts for the majority of total recorded music income in most major markets around the world.

One of the most significant effects of streaming on music consumption is the way it has changed how listeners discover new music. In the past, people typically found out about new artists through radio programs, music television channels, or recommendations from friends and family. Today, streaming platforms use sophisticated computer programs called algorithms to analyze each user's listening history and suggest new songs and artists that they are likely to enjoy. These personalized recommendation systems have made it much easier for listeners to find music that matches their tastes, but they have also been criticized for creating what some researchers call a "filter bubble" — a situation in which listeners are repeatedly shown music that is similar to what they already know, making it less likely that they will encounter genuinely new styles or unexpected artists.

The rise of streaming has also had a major impact on how music is made and released by artists. In the era of physical albums, musicians typically spent months or even years creating a full collection of songs before releasing everything together at once. Streaming platforms, however, reward artists who release music frequently, because the algorithms that recommend songs tend to favor artists who appear in listeners' feeds regularly. As a result, many musicians now release individual songs or short collections called EPs much more often than full albums, adjusting their creative schedules to work with the logic of digital platforms rather than following the traditional patterns of the music industry. This shift has been welcomed by some artists as freeing, while others have described it as putting unhealthy pressure on creativity.

Not everyone has benefited equally from the streaming revolution, however. While major artists with large numbers of followers can earn significant income from the billions of plays their songs receive each month, independent and emerging musicians often struggle to make a living from streaming alone. Most streaming platforms pay artists a very small amount — typically a fraction of a cent — for each individual play of a song, which means that a musician needs many millions of plays per month just to earn a modest income. Many smaller artists have responded to this situation by focusing more on live performances, merchandise sales, and direct fan support platforms where their audience can pay them directly, rather than relying on streaming income to sustain their careers.

Social media has become an increasingly important part of how music spreads among listeners, particularly among younger audiences. Short video platforms such as TikTok have introduced a new way for songs to go viral — a term used to describe content that spreads very quickly and widely across the internet. When a particular song becomes popular as the background music for a trending type of short video, millions of users can discover and share it within days, sometimes turning previously unknown artists into global stars almost overnight. This kind of rapid, unpredictable popularity has created new opportunities for musicians outside the traditional music industry system, but it has also made the music business more difficult to predict and plan for record labels and talent managers.

Despite all of these changes, music itself remains as important as ever to people's daily lives. Studies consistently show that people listen to music while commuting, exercising, working, and relaxing, and that music plays a central role in how people manage their emotions and connect with others. The formats and platforms through which music travels may continue to evolve rapidly, but the fundamental human need to hear and share music appears to be one of the most enduring features of modern life. Understanding how technology changes the way we access music is important, but it is equally important to remember that what drives music consumption ultimately is not the platform — it is the deep and lasting connection between listeners and the songs that matter most to them.

Để đạt kết quả tốt cho phần thi này, bạn nên áp dụng các chiến thuật sau đây:

  • Dạng câu hỏi Ý chính (R1Q1): Sử dụng kỹ năng Skimming (Đọc lướt). Đọc câu đầu đoạn 1 và câu kết bài ở đoạn 7 để nắm trọn mạch logic. Bài đọc không chỉ phiến diện về một khía cạnh như sự bất công đối với nghệ sĩ độc lập hay chỉ ca ngợi TikTok. Nó phác họa một bức tranh đa chiều: công nghệ kỹ thuật số và streaming đã tái định hình toàn diện cách tiếp cận, khám phá, sản xuất và chia sẻ âm nhạc, mang lại cả cơ hội lẫn thách thức, trong khi sợi dây kết nối cảm xúc của con người với âm nhạc vẫn là bất biến.
  • Dạng câu hỏi Chi tiết (R1Q2, R1Q3, R1Q4, R1Q6): Sử dụng kỹ năng Scanning (Đọc quét) từ khóa để xác vị trí thông tin gốc. Với R1Q2, quét đoạn 2 tìm từ khóa phí và cách thức truy cập để thấy người dùng có thể nghe kho nhạc khổng lồ bằng cách trả phí đăng ký hàng tháng hoặc nghe miễn phí kèm quảng cáo. Với R1Q3, tìm cụm từ "filter bubble" ở đoạn 3 để thấy định nghĩa của các nhà nghiên cứu: hiện tượng người nghe liên tục được gợi ý các bài hát tương tự gu cũ, làm giảm khả năng tiếp cận các phong cách mới lạ. Với R1Q4, quét đoạn 4 tìm từ khóa liên quan đến thuật toán và tần suất phát hành để thấy các thuật toán ưu ái nghệ sĩ xuất hiện đều đặn trên feed của người nghe, giúp họ duy trì độ nhận diện. Với R1Q6, quét đoạn 5 tìm từ khóa "independent musicians" để thấy cách họ phản ứng với doanh thu thấp: tập trung vào biểu diễn live, bán vật phẩm lưu niệm và dùng nền tảng ủng hộ trực tiếp.
  • Dạng câu hỏi Quy chiếu (R1Q5, R1Q7): Đọc kỹ ngữ cảnh và mối quan hệ ngữ pháp xung quanh đại từ. Với R1Q5, tính từ sở hữu "their" nằm trong cụm "matches their tastes" ở đoạn 3. Đối chiếu ngược lại danh từ số nhiều đứng ngay trước đóng vai trò chủ thể sở hữu gu âm nhạc này chính là "listeners" (người nghe). Với R1Q7, đại từ "it" ở đoạn 4 nằm trong câu "others have described it as putting unhealthy pressure on creativity". "It" ở đây thay thế cho toàn bộ xu hướng/sự dịch chuyển được thảo luận ở câu trước: việc phải phát hành các bài hát đơn lẻ hoặc EP liên tục để chiều lòng thuật toán.
  • Dạng câu hỏi Loại trừ NOT (R1Q9): Đối soát trực tiếp danh sách các chiến lược sinh tồn của nghệ sĩ độc lập tại đoạn 5. Bài viết gọi tên việc đi diễn live, bán đồ lưu niệm và quyên góp trực tiếp từ fan. Việc ký hợp đồng độc quyền với một nền tảng để nhận lương cứng hàng tháng hoàn toàn không được nhắc tới, do đó đây là đáp án đúng.
  • Dạng câu hỏi Từ vựng trong ngữ cảnh (R1Q8): Sử dụng kỹ năng phân tích Context Clues (Manh mối ngữ cảnh) ở đoạn 6. Từ "viral" được giải thích ngay trong văn bản bằng dấu gạch ngang: "spreads very quickly and widely across the internet". Do đó, nó mang nghĩa là sự lan truyền cực kỳ nhanh chóng và rộng rãi trên không gian mạng trực tuyến mà không cần đến các phương thức quảng bá truyền thống.
  • Dạng câu hỏi Suy luận (R1Q10): Đọc sâu và tổng hợp thông tin ở đoạn cuối cùng (đoạn 7). Tác giả khẳng định dù nền tảng hay định dạng công nghệ có thay đổi liên tục thế nào đi chăng nữa, thì mối liên kết sâu sắc giữa người nghe và những bài hát mới là yếu tố cốt lõi và bất biến thúc đẩy việc tiêu thụ âm nhạc.

Lời khuyên: Đây là một bài đọc có cấu trúc phân mảnh theo chủ đề rất rõ ràng và mạch lạc. Bạn nên ưu tiên làm các câu hỏi Chi tiết (R1Q2, R1Q3, R1Q4, R1Q6), câu Từ vựng (R1Q8) và các câu Quy chiếu (R1Q5, R1Q7) trước bằng kỹ thuật dò từ khóa trực tiếp. Sau khi loại trừ được phương án ở câu NOT (R1Q9), bạn sẽ có cái nhìn toàn vẹn để xử lý câu hỏi Ý chính (R1Q1) và Suy luận (R1Q10) ở lượt làm bài cuối cùng mà không sợ bị nhầm lẫn bởi các phương án nhiễu.

questions.question: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Streaming platforms have completely replaced all previous forms of music consumption and have made it impossible for independent artists to earn a living from recorded music alone.

The most important change in modern music consumption is the rise of social media platforms like TikTok, which have given unknown artists a way to become globally famous without the support of a record label.
Digital technology and streaming have transformed how music is accessed, discovered, made, and shared, bringing new opportunities and challenges while the human connection to music remains unchanged.
Independent and emerging musicians have suffered the most from the rise of streaming because the payment system used by major platforms makes it nearly impossible for them to earn a fair income.

questions.question: According to the passage, how do streaming platforms typically provide access to their music libraries?
options: Users can listen to a vast library of songs either by paying a monthly subscription fee or for free while hearing occasional advertisements between songs.
Users must purchase individual songs or albums at a fixed price before they can listen to them, with the option of requesting a refund if they are not satisfied with their purchase.
Users receive a limited number of free listening hours each month and must pay an additional fee for each hour of music they listen to beyond that monthly allowance.
Users pay a one-time fee to download an unlimited number of songs to their personal devices, where the music is stored permanently and can be listened to without an internet connection.

questions.question: According to the passage, what do some researchers mean when they describe streaming algorithms as creating a "filter bubble"?
options: A situation in which users who listen to music without paying a subscription fee are shown fewer recommendations than paying subscribers, creating an unequal experience across different types of users.

A situation in which streaming platforms prioritize music from major record labels in their recommendation algorithms, making it very difficult for independent artists to reach new listeners through the platform.

A situation in which streaming platforms remove songs containing offensive content from their recommendation systems, limiting the range of music available to users in certain countries or age groups.
A situation in which listeners are repeatedly recommended music that is similar to what they already know, reducing the likelihood that they will discover genuinely new styles or unexpected artists.

questions.question: According to the passage, why do streaming platform algorithms tend to favor artists who release music frequently?
options: Streaming platforms rank search results by the total number of songs an artist has available, so musicians who release frequently appear higher in search results and are more easily found by new listeners.

Algorithms tend to recommend artists who appear in listeners' feeds regularly, meaning that frequent releases help musicians maintain visibility and reach new audiences through the platform's recommendation system.
Streaming platforms charge artists a smaller distribution fee per song when they release music frequently, creating a financial incentive for musicians to publish new material on a regular schedule.
Listeners who use streaming platforms are more likely to pay for a monthly subscription if they notice that their favorite artists are releasing new material regularly throughout the year.

questions.question: The word "their" in paragraph 3 refers to _______.
options: radio programs and music television channels, which previously shaped the musical tastes of audiences before streaming platforms took over as the primary source of new music discovery
listeners, whose personal music tastes are analyzed by recommendation systems to suggest songs and artists that the individual is likely to find appealing
streaming platforms, which design personalized recommendation systems to match each user's listening history with algorithmically selected songs and artists from their enormous music catalogs
algorithms, which analyze individual listening data in order to develop an accurate understanding of the musical preferences associated with each user account on the platform

questions.question: According to the passage, how have many independent musicians responded to the low per-play income they receive from streaming platforms?
options: Many smaller artists have focused more on live performances, merchandise sales, and direct fan support platforms where their audience can pay them directly, rather than depending on streaming income.

Independent musicians have formed collective organizations that negotiate directly with streaming platforms for higher payment rates on behalf of artists who do not have the support of a major record label.

Many smaller artists have responded by releasing music much less frequently, concentrating their efforts on creating a small number of high-quality songs that are more likely to receive a large number of plays.

Many independent artists have chosen to remove their music from major streaming platforms entirely and distribute it exclusively through their own websites, where they can set their own prices and keep all of the revenue.

questions.question: The word "it" in paragraph 4 refers to _______.
options: the traditional full album format, which many musicians feel has been unfairly devalued by streaming platforms that reward frequent individual releases over carefully crafted long-form collections of songs
the shift toward releasing individual songs and short EPs frequently in order to remain visible in streaming algorithms, which some artists find places unhealthy pressure on their creative process

the music industry's traditional pattern of spending months or years on a full album before releasing it, which streaming platforms have effectively made commercially unviable for most working musicians
the algorithm that streaming platforms use to recommend music to listeners, which some artists believe makes unfair demands on their time by requiring them to constantly promote new releases

questions.question: The word "viral" in paragraph 6 is closest in meaning to _______.
options: spreading extremely quickly and widely among large numbers of people through online sharing, reaching a massive audience in a very short period of time without requiring traditional promotion
created specifically for a target audience of young social media users who are likely to share content that reflects their personal interests and current cultural trends
controversial or unexpected in a way that surprises audiences and generates significant discussion and debate across different online communities and social media platforms
professionally produced and promoted by a major entertainment company with a large marketing budget and established distribution networks across multiple digital and traditional media platforms

questions.question: According to the passage, which of the following strategies for earning income is NOT mentioned as a response used by independent musicians struggling with low streaming revenue?
options: Selling branded merchandise such as clothing, posters, and other products directly to their audience
Using direct fan support platforms where their audience can pay them directly to support their work
Performing live concerts and events where fans pay for tickets to see them play in person
Signing exclusive contracts with one major streaming platform in exchange for a guaranteed monthly income

questions.question: What can be inferred from the final paragraph about the author's view of the relationship between technology and music consumption?
options: The author implies that the music industry should invest less in developing new technology platforms and focus instead on helping artists build stronger direct relationships with their audiences through live performance.

The author suggests that while the platforms and formats through which people access music will keep changing, the deep human connection to music is what truly drives consumption and will remain constant.

The author argues that the rapid pace of technological change in music consumption has made it impossible for the industry to develop long-term strategies, leaving both artists and listeners in a state of constant uncertainty.

The author believes that streaming technology and social media platforms have fundamentally changed what people want from music, shifting the focus from emotional connection to convenience and novelty.

passage.title: The Daily Struggle of Peak Hour Traffic
passage.text:
In cities around the world, the morning and evening rush hours represent a daily ritual of frustration that millions of commuters endure with a mixture of resignation and quiet misery. The phenomenon of peak hour traffic — the dramatic slowdown of road networks during the hours when workers travel to and from their places of employment — has been a defining feature of urban life since the rapid expansion of automobile ownership in the mid-twentieth century. Despite decades of investment in road infrastructure, public transportation systems, and increasingly sophisticated traffic management technology, congestion during peak hours remains one of the most stubbornly persistent challenges that city planners and transport authorities face. In many of the world's largest metropolitan areas, the average commuter spends more than fifty hours per year sitting in stationary or near-stationary traffic, a figure that carries significant implications for individual well-being, economic productivity, and environmental sustainability.

The economic costs of peak hour congestion are both direct and substantial. Fuel wasted in idling vehicles, the time value of workers who arrive late or leave early to avoid the worst of the rush, the higher operating costs of delivery and logistics companies whose schedules are disrupted by unpredictable travel times, and the cumulative effect of reduced productivity across urban workforces all translate into measurable financial losses that economists have attempted to quantify with increasing precision. Studies conducted in major cities including London, São Paulo, and Bangkok have estimated that peak hour congestion costs their local economies billions of dollars annually in lost productive time alone, before factoring in the additional costs of vehicle maintenance accelerated by stop-start driving conditions, the health expenses associated with pollution from idling engines, and the strain placed on emergency services whose response times are lengthened when ambulances and fire trucks cannot move freely through congested streets.

The psychological toll of regular commuting in heavy traffic is less frequently discussed but no less significant. Research in environmental psychology and occupational health has consistently demonstrated that long, unpredictable commutes are among the most reliably stressful daily experiences that urban residents face. Unlike other stressors that individuals can prepare for or respond to actively, traffic congestion is largely outside the commuter's control — a fact that makes it particularly damaging to emotional well-being. Studies tracking the mood and stress hormone levels of regular commuters have found that people who spend more than thirty minutes each way in heavy traffic report significantly lower levels of life satisfaction and significantly higher rates of anxiety, sleep disruption, and interpersonal conflict at home than those with shorter or less congested commutes. The commute's capacity to poison the hours that precede and follow it — arriving at work already exhausted, returning home already irritable — compounds its impact well beyond the journey itself.

Attempts by city governments to reduce peak hour congestion have followed several broad strategies, none of which has proven entirely sufficient on its own. Expanding road capacity through the construction of additional lanes, ring roads, and bypass routes was the dominant approach in many cities through the latter half of the twentieth century, but transport economists have identified a well-documented phenomenon known as induced demand: when new road capacity is added, it tends to attract additional vehicle trips that fill the new space, returning congestion to levels similar to those that existed before the expansion. Public transportation investment — in metro rail systems, bus rapid transit corridors, and light rail networks — has proven more effective at reducing car dependency in cities where services are frequent, reliable, and well-integrated with the areas of highest commuter density. However, the upfront capital costs of high-quality public transit infrastructure are substantial, and the decades-long timelines required for major projects to be planned, funded, and built mean that transport solutions are frequently overtaken by population growth before they are completed.

Congestion pricing — the practice of charging drivers a fee to enter the most congested parts of a city during peak hours — has emerged as one of the most economically rational tools available to urban transport authorities, and several cities have implemented versions of it with measurable success. Stockholm introduced a congestion charge in 2006 following a successful trial period, and the city recorded a sustained reduction in vehicle entries to the charged zone of approximately twenty percent, along with improvements in public transport usage and air quality. London's congestion charge, introduced in 2003, has similarly reduced traffic volumes in the central zone, though its effects have been partially offset by the growth of ride-hailing services whose vehicles spend significant time cruising without passengers in the charged area. The political challenges of implementing congestion pricing, however, are considerable: the charge is perceived by many drivers as an additional tax on commuting, and it has faced significant public opposition in cities where private car use is deeply embedded in daily life and culture.

The COVID-19 pandemic provided an unplanned but revealing natural experiment in what urban traffic patterns might look like if a significant proportion of office workers shifted permanently to remote or hybrid working arrangements. During the strictest phases of lockdown, traffic volumes in major cities fell by fifty percent or more, producing dramatic and almost immediate improvements in air quality, journey times for essential workers, and noise levels in previously congested urban neighborhoods. As restrictions lifted and workers gradually returned to offices, congestion rebounded — but not uniformly. In cities where employers embraced hybrid working schedules that stagger office attendance across different days of the week, the sharpness of the traditional Monday-to-Friday morning and evening peaks has been noticeably reduced, suggesting that relatively modest changes in the temporal distribution of commuter journeys can produce disproportionately large improvements in network performance.

The future of peak hour traffic is likely to be shaped by the interaction of several forces that are currently in early stages of development: the continued expansion of remote and hybrid working norms, the gradual introduction of autonomous and connected vehicle technology that may improve the flow efficiency of road networks, the electrification of vehicle fleets that addresses emissions but not congestion itself, and the evolution of urban land use patterns as housing, employment, and services redistribute in response to changing commuter behavior. What is clear, regardless of which of these forces ultimately proves most influential, is that the daily experience of peak hour congestion is as much a product of how cities are organized and how work is structured as it is a consequence of any particular failure of transport infrastructure — and that the most durable solutions are likely to require changes at all of these levels simultaneously rather than within any single domain alone.

tasks.suggestion:
Để đạt kết quả tốt cho phần thi này, bạn nên áp dụng các chiến thuật sau đây:

  • Dạng câu hỏi Ý chính & Mục đích tác giả (R2Q1, R2Q10): Sử dụng kỹ năng Skimming (Đọc lướt). Đọc câu đầu đoạn 1 và toàn bộ đoạn 7 để nắm trọn vẹn mạch logic của tác giả. Với R2Q1, bài đọc phân tích toàn diện vấn đề giao thông giờ cao điểm từ tác động kinh tế, tâm lý đến các giải pháp thực tế; do đó phương án phản ánh chính xác lập luận trung tâm: đây là một thách thức đô thị dai dẳng cần những giải pháp đồng bộ từ hạ tầng, cấu trúc công việc đến tổ chức thành phố. Với R2Q10, ở đoạn cuối tác giả không tập trung dự đoán công nghệ đơn lẻ mà nhằm kết luận rằng giải pháp bền vững phải là sự thay đổi đồng thời trên nhiều phương diện chứ không thể chỉ phụ thuộc vào một yếu tố duy nhất.
  • Dạng câu hỏi Chi tiết (R2Q2, R2Q4, R2Q5): Sử dụng kỹ năng Scanning (Đọc quét) để định vị nhanh vùng thông tin chứa từ khóa. Với R2Q2, quét đoạn 2 tìm các tổn thất kinh tế để thấy bài đọc nhắc trực tiếp đến thiệt hại tài chính của các công ty vận tải và logistics do thời gian di chuyển không thể dự đoán trước. Với R2Q4, quét đoạn 4 tìm thuật ngữ "induced demand" (cầu cảm ứng) để hiểu bản chất của nó: việc mở rộng đường sẽ vô tình thu hút thêm lượng phương tiện mới đổ về, khiến tình trạng tắc nghẽn nhanh chóng quay lại mức cũ. Với R2Q5, quét đoạn 5 tìm từ khóa "Stockholm" và năm "2006" để xác định số liệu thực tế: giảm khoảng 20% lượng xe đi vào vùng thu phí, đồng thời cải thiện chất lượng không khí và tăng lượng dùng phương tiện công cộng.
  • Dạng câu hỏi Từ vựng trong ngữ cảnh (R2Q3): Sử dụng kỹ năng phân tích Context Clues (Manh mối ngữ cảnh) ở đoạn 2. Từ "cumulative" đứng trước "effect of reduced productivity" (hệ quả tích lũy của việc giảm năng suất) nằm trong chuỗi các tổn thất, mang nghĩa là sự cộng dồn, tích tụ tăng tiến dần theo thời gian từ nhiều đóng góp nhỏ lẻ để tạo ra một tác động tổng thể lớn hơn.
  • Dạng câu hỏi Quy chiếu (R2Q6): Đọc kỹ toàn bộ câu chứa đại từ ở đoạn 3. Đại từ sở hữu "its" nằm trong cụm "compounds its impact well beyond the journey itself" (làm trầm trọng hơn tác động của nó vượt ra ngoài bản thân hành trình). Dựa vào chủ ngữ chính ở đầu câu "The commute's capacity to poison...", từ "its" quy chiếu trực tiếp đến "the commute" (hành trình đi làm).
  • Dạng câu hỏi Loại trừ NOT (R2Q7): Tiến hành đối soát các giải pháp được liệt kê ở đoạn 4 và 5. Bài đọc nhắc đến mở rộng đường, đầu tư metro/BRT, và tối ưu phương tiện công cộng tại các vùng mật độ cao. Phương án yêu cầu các công ty bắt buộc phải áp dụng chính sách so le giờ làm việc của nhân viên hoàn toàn không được nhắc đến như một chiến lược của chính quyền thành phố trong đoạn này, do đó đây là đáp án cần chọn.
  • Dạng câu hỏi Suy luận (R2Q8, R2Q9): Kết hợp và tổng hợp thông tin một cách logic. questions.question: What is the main argument of the passage?
options: Congestion pricing is the most effective tool available to city governments for reducing peak hour traffic because it directly changes the behavior of drivers and generates revenue that can be reinvested in public transportation.

Peak hour traffic is a persistent urban challenge with wide-ranging economic, psychological, and environmental consequences whose most durable solutions require simultaneous changes to transport infrastructure, work structures, and city organization.

The COVID-19 pandemic demonstrated that remote working is the most powerful solution to peak hour congestion, and governments should make permanent hybrid working arrangements mandatory for all office-based employees.

Peak hour congestion is primarily an infrastructure problem that can be solved through a combination of road expansion and investment in high-quality public transportation systems in cities where car ownership is high.

questions.question: According to the passage, which of the following economic costs of peak hour congestion is mentioned in the passage?
options: The cost of constructing additional road lanes and bypass routes to increase the capacity of urban transport networks in cities that have experienced rapid population growth
The financial losses incurred by logistics and delivery companies whose operating schedules are disrupted by the unpredictable journey times caused by peak hour congestion
The cost to municipal governments of hiring additional traffic management personnel to monitor and direct vehicle flow through the most congested intersections during morning and evening rush hours
The reduction in property values in urban neighborhoods located close to heavily congested arterial roads that experience high levels of noise and air pollution throughout the working week

questions.question: The word "cumulative" in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to _______.
options: building up progressively through the accumulation of many individual contributions over time, producing a total effect that is larger than any single instance would suggest
immediate and concentrated, producing its full economic impact at a single point in time rather than building gradually across multiple interactions over an extended period
difficult to measure precisely because it results from the interaction of multiple independent variables that affect the urban economy in ways that resist straightforward quantification
distributed unevenly across different sectors of the urban economy, with some industries absorbing a disproportionately large share of the total losses caused by peak hour congestion

questions.question: According to the passage, what does the economic phenomenon known as "induced demand" suggest about the effectiveness of expanding road capacity to reduce congestion?
options: Expanding road capacity reduces congestion only in the short term before drivers adjust their departure times to take advantage of the improved conditions, restoring peak hour volumes to their previous levels.
Road expansion projects take so long to complete that population growth during the construction period typically eliminates any congestion benefits before the new infrastructure is opened to traffic.

New road capacity tends to attract additional vehicle trips that fill the expanded space, returning congestion to levels similar to those before the expansion and undermining the investment's intended purpose.

The benefits of road expansion are limited to the specific routes that are widened, causing traffic to redistribute onto parallel streets and creating new congestion problems in areas that previously flowed freely.

questions.question: According to the passage, what measurable outcome did Stockholm record following the introduction of its congestion charge in 2006?
options: The city recorded a sustained reduction of approximately twenty percent in vehicle entries to the charged zone, along with improvements in public transport usage and air quality.

Journey times for commuters entering the charged zone fell by an average of thirty percent during peak hours, making Stockholm one of the fastest-improving cities in Europe for urban road transport efficiency.
Revenue generated by the congestion charge was used to fund a major expansion of the city's metro rail network, which produced the most significant long-term reductions in peak hour road traffic.

Vehicle entries to the charged zone fell by approximately fifty percent, and the city recorded a significant increase in cycling and walking as commuters sought alternatives to both driving and public transport.

questions.question: The word "its" in paragraph 3 refers to _______.
options: stress, whose capacity to spread from the journey itself into the hours that surround it is what makes long commutes more harmful to well-being than other daily stressors of equivalent duration
heavy traffic, whose unpredictable and uncontrollable nature is identified as the primary reason why congestion is particularly damaging to the emotional well-being of regular urban commuters

the commute, whose ability to affect the quality of the hours before and after the journey itself amplifies its total impact on mood, energy, and interpersonal relationships beyond the travel time alone
the commuter, whose emotional state after a difficult journey in heavy traffic affects not only their own well-being but also the atmosphere of both their workplace and their home environment

questions.question: According to the passage, which of the following approaches to reducing peak hour congestion is NOT mentioned as a strategy that city governments have attempted?
options: Developing public transportation services that are frequent, reliable, and well-integrated with the areas of highest commuter density
Investing in metro rail systems, bus rapid transit corridors, and light rail networks to provide alternatives to private car travel
Introducing flexible working hour policies that require employers to stagger their employees' start and finish times to spread commuter journeys more evenly across the day
Building additional road lanes, ring roads, and bypass routes to increase the total capacity of urban road networks

questions.question: What can be inferred from paragraph 6 about the relationship between the timing of commuter journeys and road network performance?
options: Even relatively modest changes in when commuters travel — spreading journeys more evenly across different days of the week — can produce disproportionately large improvements in network performance by reducing the sharpness of traditional peaks.

The improvements in traffic conditions observed during COVID-19 lockdowns were entirely temporary and provided no useful information about how urban transport systems might be managed differently in normal conditions.

The evidence from the pandemic period suggests that only a complete elimination of commuting through permanent remote working can produce meaningful and lasting improvements in peak hour traffic conditions.

The pandemic data suggests that a reduction of fifty percent or more in total vehicle volumes is the minimum threshold required to produce meaningful improvements in journey times for essential workers.

questions.question: What can be inferred from paragraphs 4 and 5 about why no single strategy for reducing peak hour congestion has proven entirely sufficient on its own?
options: Each strategy addresses only a specific dimension of the congestion problem while generating its own limitations or unintended consequences, meaning that the complexity of the challenge requires a combination of approaches rather than any single intervention.

Congestion reduction strategies work well in cities with specific geographic or demographic characteristics but cannot be successfully transferred to cities with different urban layouts, population densities, or commuter behavior patterns.

Individual congestion reduction strategies are undermined by the political difficulty of implementing them, since most measures that would effectively reduce traffic volumes are unpopular with the drivers whose behavior they are designed to change.

The most effective strategies for reducing congestion — particularly congestion pricing and public transit investment — are too expensive for most city governments to implement at the scale required to produce meaningful results.

questions.question: What is the author's purpose in the final paragraph of the passage?
options: To predict that autonomous vehicle technology will be the most transformative force shaping the future of urban traffic and will ultimately eliminate peak hour congestion without requiring changes to how cities are organized or how work is structured.

To argue that the electrification of vehicle fleets is the most urgent priority for city governments because it addresses both the emissions and the congestion dimensions of the peak hour traffic problem simultaneously.

To suggest that the future of peak hour traffic is too uncertain to plan for effectively, and that city governments should focus on managing current congestion rather than investing in solutions whose impact cannot be reliably predicted.

To conclude that peak hour congestion is as much a consequence of how cities are organized and how work is structured as of infrastructure failure, and that durable solutions will require simultaneous change across multiple domains rather than within any single one.

passage.title: The Weight of Success: Modern Youth and Societal Pressure
passage.text:
Adolescence has always carried its share of difficulty — the physical changes of puberty, the social turbulence of peer relationships, the early encounters with failure and disappointment that form the emotional foundation of adult life. Yet developmental psychologists and youth mental health researchers have, with growing consistency over the past two decades, identified something qualitatively different about the pressures facing young people in the early twenty-first century. The convergence of hypercompetitive academic environments, algorithmically amplified social comparison, economically anxious parenting cultures, and the dissolution of unstructured leisure time has produced, across multiple high-income countries, a measurable deterioration in adolescent psychological well-being that represents one of the most consequential public health developments of the contemporary period. What distinguishes this moment from earlier periods of perceived youth crisis is the robustness of the epidemiological evidence: rates of diagnosed anxiety disorders, clinical depression, and self-reported psychological distress among teenagers have risen significantly and persistently across countries with widely different cultural traditions, suggesting that the drivers of this trend are structural rather than idiosyncratic. [1]

The academic dimension of this pressure system deserves particular scrutiny because it operates through institutions — schools, examination boards, universities — that are generally understood to serve the developmental interests of young people but that have, in significant respects, been restructured in ways that prioritize measurable performance outcomes over the psychological conditions under which genuine learning and intellectual curiosity can flourish. In many educational systems, the pressure to accumulate high-stakes examination results begins earlier than it did for previous generations, extends across a wider range of subjects and co-curricular domains, and is communicated to students with greater urgency and consequence. The message that academic credentials function as gating mechanisms for life outcomes — determining university admission, career trajectory, and economic security — is absorbed by students with increasing literalness, producing a relationship with learning that is instrumentalized rather than intrinsically motivated. Researchers studying academic motivation have documented a troubling shift: students who once described learning as enjoyable increasingly describe it as a performance to be managed, an anxiety to be survived, rather than an experience to be had. [2]

The role of digital technology — and social media platforms in particular — in intensifying the social comparison pressures that adolescents experience has been extensively studied and is now reasonably well established in the research literature, though the precise causal mechanisms remain a matter of active debate. What is not in dispute is that social media platforms provide adolescents with an unprecedented quantity of information about how their peers are performing, appearing, achieving, and being perceived — information that is systematically skewed toward the curated highlights of others' lives rather than their authentic daily experience. The result is a social comparison environment qualitatively different from anything previous generations navigated: one in which the reference group is not limited to the thirty students in a classroom or the dozen friends in a neighborhood, but potentially encompasses hundreds of peers whose most flattering self-presentations are visible at any hour. Research by the developmental psychologist Jean Twenge has tracked the correlation between the rise of smartphone adoption among teenagers and the simultaneous deterioration of adolescent well-being indicators across multiple countries, a correlation that has proven robust across different methodological approaches even as scholars debate the magnitude of the effect. [3]

Parenting culture has itself undergone a transformation that amplifies the pressures described above rather than buffering young people against them. The emergence of what sociologist Annette Lareau termed "concerted cultivation" — an approach to child-rearing prevalent among middle and upper-middle class families that treats childhood as a project of deliberate development, filling available time with structured activities, tutoring programs, and resume-building experiences — has produced childhoods that are, by several measurable indicators, more enriched and more anxious simultaneously. The logic of concerted cultivation holds that parental investment in children's skills, credentials, and social capital is the responsible response to an economically competitive environment in which the consequences of falling behind are severe. The consequence, documented across qualitative studies of adolescent experience, is that many young people internalize the developmental project as their own imperative — experiencing the absence of productivity not as rest but as failure, and struggling to access the unstructured, unsupervised exploration that developmental research identifies as essential to the formation of autonomous identity and intrinsic motivation.

The health consequences of sustained performance pressure during adolescence extend considerably beyond the psychological symptoms most commonly associated with stress. Sleep deprivation — driven by late-night studying, device use, and the physiological effects of chronic anxiety — has reached levels in high-achieving adolescent populations that clinical researchers describe as a public health concern in its own right. Studies tracking the academic schedules of students in competitive secondary schools have found that a substantial proportion regularly sleep fewer than six hours per night during examination periods, a pattern associated not only with impaired cognitive performance on the assessments they are sacrificing sleep to prepare for but also with increased risk of depression, immune system suppression, and metabolic disruption. The irony that the behaviors most commonly adopted in pursuit of academic success may systematically undermine the cognitive capacities that academic performance depends upon is one that educational researchers have documented with considerable precision but that has proven difficult to translate into meaningful changes in institutional practice. [4]

Responses to the adolescent mental health crisis have emerged at multiple levels, with varying degrees of evidence for their effectiveness. School-based mindfulness programs, social-emotional learning curricula, and peer support networks have demonstrated positive effects in controlled studies, though their impact is typically modest relative to the scale of the pressures students face and their benefits tend to be concentrated among students who are already relatively resilient. More structurally ambitious interventions — reforming examination systems to reduce high-stakes testing frequency, delaying school start times to align with adolescent sleep biology, and redesigning university admissions processes to reduce the credential arms race among applicants — have proven politically difficult to implement at scale despite compelling evidence for their effectiveness. The gap between what the research evidence supports and what educational and political institutions are willing to implement reflects a broader tension between the structural drivers of adolescent pressure and the individualized frameworks through which mental health is most commonly addressed in policy.

What the accumulation of research on modern adolescent pressure ultimately points toward is a recognition that the psychological difficulties facing young people today are not primarily the product of individual vulnerability or inadequate coping skills — the framing that dominates clinical and self-help discourse on youth mental health — but of environments that have been systematically structured to produce exactly the outcomes they are now generating. A young person who experiences chronic anxiety about academic performance in a system that communicates high stakes at every turn, who compares herself unfavorably to algorithmically curated peer presentations on social media, and who has been raised in a parenting culture that frames productivity as the primary measure of worth is responding rationally to her environment. The challenge is not to make her more resilient in the face of these pressures but to reconstruct the environments — educational, digital, familial — in which she is developing, so that they support rather than undermine the psychological foundations of a flourishing human life.

tasks.suggestion:
Để đạt kết quả tốt cho phần thi này, bạn nên áp dụng các chiến thuật sau đây:

  • Dạng câu hỏi Ý chính & Thái độ tác giả (R3Q1, R3Q9): Sử dụng kỹ năng Skimming (Đọc lướt). Đọc câu đầu đoạn 1 và phần kết luận ở đoạn 7 để nắm luận điểm cốt lõi. Với R3Q1, bài viết tập trung chứng minh rằng khủng hoảng sức khỏe tâm thần của giới trẻ không phải do sự yếu kém cá nhân mà là hệ quả từ các môi trường — giáo dục, kỹ thuật số, và gia đình — vốn được cấu trúc một cách có hệ thống làm xói mòn các điều kiện phát triển lành mạnh. Với R3Q9, dựa vào cách tác giả lập luận ở đoạn 6-7, học sinh chỉ đang phản ứng một cách hợp lý ("responding rationally") trước các áp lực từ môi trường, do đó giải pháp đúng đắn là phải tái cấu trúc lại các môi trường đó thay vì chỉ bắt cá nhân phải gia tăng sức chịu đựng.
  • Dạng câu hỏi Chi tiết (R3Q2, R3Q4, R3Q5, R3Q6): Sử dụng kỹ năng Scanning (Đọc quét) từ khóa để khoanh vùng thông tin gốc. Với R3Q2, tìm từ khóa "relationship with learning" ở đoạn 2 để thấy sự dịch chuyển đáng ngại: học sinh từ chỗ coi việc học là niềm vui dần chuyển sang nhìn nhận nó như một buổi biểu diễn cần phải xoay sở và một nỗi bất an cần phải sống sót vượt qua. With R3Q4, quét đoạn 4 tìm thuật ngữ "concerted cultivation" (nuôi dưỡng có chủ đích) để thấy nghịch lý: giới trẻ vô tình biến dự án phát triển này thành nghĩa vụ cá nhân, coi việc thiếu năng suất là thất bại và đánh mất đi không gian khám phá tự do cần thiết. Với R3Q5, quét đoạn 5 tìm từ khóa "sleep deprivation" để chỉ ra sự trớ trêu: chính những hành vi thức khuya học bài để mưu cầu thành công học thuật lại đang tàn phá một cách hệ thống các năng lực nhận thức mà kết quả học tập phụ thuộc vào. Với R3Q6, quét đoạn 6 để tìm nguyên nhân các cải cách cấu trúc (lùi giờ học, cải cách thi cử) chưa được áp dụng rộng rãi: do chúng gặp phải sự cản trở về mặt chính trị và thách thức các cấu trúc thể chế cùng kỳ vọng văn hóa đã bám rễ sâu.
  • Dạng câu hỏi Từ vựng trong ngữ cảnh (R3Q3, R3Q7): Sử dụng kỹ năng phân tích Context Clues (Manh mối ngữ cảnh). Với R3Q3, từ "robust" ở đoạn 3 bổ nghĩa cho số liệu/mối tương quan nghiên cứu của Jean Twenge, đi kèm cụm "across different methodological approaches". Trong nghiên cứu, từ này mang nghĩa là mạnh mẽ, nhất quán và có tính thuyết phục cao, đứng vững trước các phương pháp phân tích khác nhau. Với R3Q7, từ "idiosyncratic" ở đoạn 1 nằm trong cấu trúc đối lập trực tiếp: "structural rather than idiosyncratic" (mang tính cấu trúc hệ thống chứ không phải...). Do đó, nó mang nghĩa là mang tính cá biệt, đặc thù hoặc ngẫu nhiên theo từng bối cảnh cụ thể.
  • Dạng câu hỏi Quy chiếu (R3Q8): Đọc kỹ toàn bộ câu chứa đại từ ở đoạn 2. Đại từ "it" nằm trong cụm "increasingly describe it as a performance to be managed". Đối chiếu với vế trước "Students who once described learning as enjoyable...", ta thấy rõ ràng "it" dùng để quy chiếu trực tiếp thay thế cho danh từ "learning" (việc học) được nhắc đến ngay trước đó.
  • Dạng câu hỏi Chèn câu (R3Q10): Câu cần chèn mở đầu bằng cụm từ liên kết "This convergence..." (Sự hội tụ này) và nói về việc các bộ ngành chính thức xếp sức khỏe tâm thần giới trẻ vào nhóm lo ngại mang tính hệ thống ("systemic concern"). Vị trí [1] ở cuối đoạn 1 là hoàn hảo nhất, vì đoạn 1 vừa trình bày xong sự hội tụ của hàng loạt áp lực và đưa ra kết luận các tác nhân này mang tính "structural" (cấu trúc). Câu chèn này sẽ cụ thể hóa phản ứng mang tính thể chế đối với kết luận đó trước khi chuyển sang đoạn 2 phân tích sâu chi tiết.

Lời khuyên: Đây là bài đọc có mật độ từ vựng học thuật cao về tâm lý học và xã hội học, cấu trúc các câu lựa chọn tương đối dài. Bạn nên làm các câu hỏi Từ vựng (R3Q3, R3Q7) và câu Quy chiếu (R3Q8) trước để lấy điểm nhanh. Sau đó tiến hành quét thông tin cho các câu Chi tiết (R3Q2, R3Q4, R3Q5, R3Q6). Khi mạch lập luận toàn bài đã sáng tỏ, các câu mang tính vĩ mô như Ý chính (R3Q1), Thái độ (R3Q9) và Chèn câu (R3Q10) sẽ được giải quyết rất mượt mà.

questions.question: What is the central argument of the passage?
options: The adolescent mental health crisis is primarily the result of individual psychological vulnerability and inadequate coping skills that could be addressed through expanded access to school-based counseling and clinical intervention programs.

The deterioration of adolescent psychological well-being in contemporary societies is the product of environments — educational, digital, and familial — that have been systematically structured in ways that undermine rather than support the conditions for healthy youth development.

The most effective response to modern adolescent pressure is to reform university admissions processes and reduce high-stakes examination frequency, since these institutional structures are the primary source of the performance anxiety that drives psychological distress among teenagers.

Social media platforms are the single most important driver of the adolescent mental health crisis because they expose teenagers to social comparison pressures that previous generations were fully protected from by the geographic limits of their peer networks.

questions.question: According to the passage, what troubling shift in students' relationship with learning have researchers documented in high-pressure academic environments?
options: Students who once described learning as enjoyable increasingly describe it as a performance to be managed and an anxiety to be survived, reflecting a shift from intrinsic motivation to instrumentalized engagement with academic work.

Students have become increasingly dependent on teacher guidance and external validation to confirm their academic progress, losing the capacity for independent study and self-directed learning that university-level education requires.

Students have become significantly less willing to take intellectual risks or explore topics outside the examination curriculum, leading to a narrowing of the subjects they engage with and a decline in interdisciplinary thinking.

Students in high-pressure academic environments have developed a growing preference for memorization-based learning strategies over deep conceptual understanding because memorization produces more reliable results on standardized examinations.

questions.question: The word "robust" in paragraph 3 is closest in meaning to _______.
options: limited in its applicability, applying only to adolescents in specific demographic groups or geographic regions rather than representing a universal pattern across the full range of teenagers studied

complex in its structure, involving multiple interacting variables that must be considered simultaneously to understand the relationship between smartphone adoption and adolescent well-being deterioration

consistent and resistant to challenge, holding up reliably across different research methods and analytical approaches rather than being an artifact of any particular way of measuring the relationship

surprising in its magnitude, exceeding the predictions of the researchers who first identified the correlation and prompting a significant reassessment of the role of digital technology in adolescent development

questions.question: According to the passage, what paradox does the "concerted cultivation" approach to parenting produce in the adolescents raised under it?
options: Children raised through concerted cultivation develop stronger academic credentials and social networks than their peers but consistently underperform on measures of creative thinking and independent problem-solving that employers increasingly value.

Children raised through concerted cultivation perform well during their school years but experience a pronounced collapse of motivation and purpose during the transition to university, where the external structure their development depended on is suddenly removed.

Adolescents from concerted cultivation families develop high levels of academic motivation but low levels of social resilience, making them more vulnerable to interpersonal conflict and friendship difficulties than peers from less intensively managed childhoods.

Young people raised through concerted cultivation internalize the developmental project as their own imperative, experiencing the absence of productivity as failure and losing access to the unstructured exploration that research identifies as essential for autonomous identity formation.

questions.question: According to the passage, what is the specific irony that educational researchers have documented regarding sleep deprivation in high-achieving adolescents?
options: Students who sacrifice sleep to prepare for examinations perform worse on those assessments than peers who sleep adequately, but the belief that additional study time compensates for lost sleep is so widespread that the evidence has not changed student behavior.

The behaviors most commonly adopted in pursuit of academic success — including late-night studying that produces chronic sleep deprivation — may systematically undermine the cognitive capacities that academic performance depends upon.

questions.question: According to the passage, why have structurally ambitious interventions such as examination reform and delayed school start times not been widely implemented despite evidence of their effectiveness?
options: These interventions have proven politically difficult to implement at scale because they challenge established institutional structures and cultural expectations, even though the research evidence for their effectiveness is compelling.

Parents from middle and upper-middle class backgrounds actively oppose structural reforms that would reduce academic pressure on their children because they believe that competitive academic environments provide an essential advantage in university admissions.

Teachers and school administrators resist structural reforms because changes to examination frequency and school schedules would significantly increase their workload without producing corresponding improvements in measurable student performance outcomes.

Educational authorities lack the financial resources to implement structural reforms at scale because the costs of redesigning examination systems and changing school schedules are prohibitive given current public education budgets.

questions.question: The word "idiosyncratic" in paragraph 1 is closest in meaning to _______.
options: well-documented and widely acknowledged among researchers, having been studied sufficiently to establish a clear causal relationship between specific environmental factors and deteriorating adolescent outcomes
specific to particular contexts or cases rather than reflecting a systematic pattern, suggesting that local or individual factors rather than shared structural conditions are primarily responsible

temporary and self-correcting, likely to resolve without institutional intervention as social and economic conditions change and adolescents develop more effective strategies for managing competitive environments

politically sensitive and resistant to public discussion, making it difficult for researchers and policymakers to address the issue openly without generating controversy and opposition from affected communities

questions.question: In paragraph 2, the word "it" in the phrase "describe it as a performance to be managed" refers to _______.
options: the credential-gathering process, which students describe as a performance because it requires them to present themselves strategically to universities and employers rather than authentically
the high-stakes examination system, which students increasingly experience as a performance event rather than a genuine assessment of their knowledge, skills, and intellectual development
academic pressure, which students report managing as a performance rather than addressing directly because the underlying anxiety it generates feels too overwhelming to confront honestly
learning itself, which students who once found enjoyable now increasingly experience as something to perform and survive rather than as an intrinsically rewarding intellectual activity

questions.question: Which of the following best characterizes the author's stance toward adolescents who experience chronic anxiety about academic performance?
